An outage not valued in kWh does not enter the denominator, so availability is HIGHER than reality. This is the group to deal with first.
An outage not valued in kWh does NOT enter the denominator. Availability is therefore higher than reality — this figure is how much higher.
AS WE measure it: actual energy ÷ (actual + lost). It counts EVERY cause, because we really do lose the energy whoever is at fault.
The share of lost energy attributable to the O&M contract. Stored separately so that BOTH availability figures trace back to one set of data.
The span from the synchronisation point to the disconnection point. DIFFERENT from the hours actually generating: a unit that stops mid-day and restarts still lies within the same span.
THE VENDOR'S FIGURE, entered from their report — the system CANNOT compute it, because what is excluded is a matter agreed in the contract rather than a calculation.
The vendor deducts fewer causes than we do, so their column is usually higher. It is precisely that gap that goes to the meeting — merge the two columns and it disappears.
%(a)d units are declared, but the availability denominator is using %(b)d. The two figures describe the same thing — a difference means one of them is declared wrongly.
The running total adds only the days that HAVE a figure. With days missing it is lower than reality — which is why it is printed beside the total rather than hidden to make the sum look seamless.
A level for scanning by eye, NOT a contract threshold — every O&M contract commits to its own figure, and assessment against the commitment happens in Contracts ▸ Assessment & payment.
Marked %(a)d locations as units (they have an energy tag). Skipped %(b)d locations with no energy tag — look again if any of them is a unit whose meter has not been attached.

Takes the ABSOLUTE value of the difference. The vendor usually deducts fewer causes, so the difference is usually positive, but a NEGATIVE one is even more worth looking at — it means the vendor claims less than we do.
The plant declares no units. Open the plant record and press "Mark units by their tags", or tick them by hand — the system does NOT guess, because guessing puts the weather station into the table.
The plant-level figure answers "how much did the site generate\n yesterday". This table answers the question the operator asks every\n morning: which machine is dragging the site down.

The mean at THIS unit, not at the weather station. Two towers five hundred metres apart can differ by a whole metre per second, and that is exactly what this column is for: explaining why two towers of the same model generate differently.

AC energy divided by DC energy over the day. Computed on the whole day's ENERGY rather than by averaging instantaneous efficiencies: efficiency at low load drags the average down even though almost no energy was produced during that stretch.

No rows usually means the plant has not declared its units. Open the plant record and press Mark units by their tags — the system does not guess, because guessing puts the weather station into the table.

Turbines and inverters — the things that actually generate. A weather station or a control building does NOT, even though they are equipment locations too. This flag decides how many rows the unit performance table has, and how many units go into the availability denominator.

The two availability columns are deliberately NOT merged. Ours counts every cause, because we really do lose the energy; the vendor's excludes what is not their responsibility. The gap is what goes to the meeting.

Deducts only the losses attributable to the contractor — THIS is the figure that agrees with the plant availability register and with the O&M contract period. The column to its left deducts EVERY cause, because we really do lose the energy whoever is at fault. The two figures answer two different questions, so it is right that they DIFFER — having only one of them is what makes people argue at cross purposes.
